strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: robustness of amortized Bayesian inference under model misspecification and out-of-simulation data.
Proposes a semi-supervised ABI approach that combines the standard simulation-based loss with a Bayesian self-consistency loss on unlabeled data, avoiding the need for true parameters for those data.

Provides theoretical results (Propositions 1–4) showing strict properness of self-consistency losses when either the likelihood or posterior is known, and of the semi-supervised loss under known likelihood; these give some formal justification for the method.

Initial experiments on the multivariate Gaussian normal means problem show large robustness gains, including for up to 100 dimensions, with very few unlabeled observations, with a summary network, and with an estimated likelihood.

The paper is generally clear about its proof-of-concept status and openly discusses some limitations, such as reduced accuracy with an estimated likelihood and issues with free-form density estimators.
weaknesses: Evaluation is far too limited for a top-tier conference: only one simple synthetic model class (multivariate Gaussian normal means) is tested. There are no experiments on other model classes, challenging posterior geometries, common SBI benchmarks, real-world data, or truly high-dimensional settings, despite promises of such experiments in the full version.

No comparison is made to existing robust ABI methods (e.g., Ward et al. 2022, Siahkoohi et al. 2023, Wehenkel et al. 2024, Gao et al. 2023, Gloeckler et al. 2023). The only baseline is standard NPE without the self-consistency loss, so the relative contribution of the proposed method is unclear.

The theoretical novelty is limited: self-consistency losses and their properness properties build heavily on prior work [22,34]. The added propositions are straightforward and rely on idealized assumptions such as a known likelihood and proposal support covering the posterior support.

The joint estimation of both posterior and likelihood is not handled rigorously. The paper acknowledges that the self-consistency loss is not strictly proper when both are unknown, but still reports improvements without clearly specifying the full training objective or explaining residual biases (e.g., reversed posterior SD bias).

The experimental design may not adequately mimic realistic out-of-simulation or real-world usage. Unlabeled data are generated from a Gaussian with the same likelihood variance as training, while evaluation observations use a much smaller variance (0.01), so the unlabeled data are not drawn from the same distribution as the test observations; no real data are used despite the motivation.

Reproducibility is insufficient: no code, data, seeds, or compute details are provided, and there is no analysis of training time or computational overhead despite the self-consistency loss requiring repeated density evaluations.

The paper overclaims its significance with phrases such as 'major breakthrough' and 'no trade-off' based on proof-of-concept experiments on a single simple model. The evidence does not support such strong general claims.

Several key experimental factors are varied only in isolation, with no ablations on the loss weight λ, proposal distribution p_C(θ), or interactions among dimensions, unlabeled sample size, and likelihood uncertainty.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: robustness of amortized Bayesian inference under distribution shift and model misspecification.

Proposes a principled semi-supervised objective that combines a standard simulation-based loss with a Bayesian self-consistency loss on unlabeled data, avoiding the need for true parameter labels for the extra data.
Provides theoretical results showing strict properness of self-consistency losses when either the likelihood or posterior is known, and for the combined semi-supervised loss.
The normal means experiments show large improvements over standard NPE, including with few unlabeled observations and in dimensions up to 100, which is a promising proof-of-concept signal.
Method preserves amortized inference and does not require post hoc corrections or labeled real-world calibration data, making it conceptually attractive.
The paper is generally clear in its method exposition and positions itself relative to several existing robust ABI approaches.
The use of an analytic posterior in the case study enables precise bias and MMD evaluation, which is appropriate for a controlled toy problem.
The self-consistency idea is extended to estimated likelihood and summary-network settings, although with reduced performance.
weaknesses: Evaluation is far too narrow for a top-tier AI conference: only a multivariate Gaussian normal means problem is tested. There is no real-world data, no benchmark simulator, no complex model class, no non-Gaussian posterior geometry, and no serious model misspecification.

The out-of-simulation setup is essentially a mean shift in a well-specified Gaussian likelihood, not a compelling model misspecification or real domain shift. The claim that the method can use data from any source, including real-world data, is not empirically demonstrated.

Missing baselines: the paper compares only against standard NPE. It does not compare against existing robust ABI methods such as adversarial training, post hoc corrections, generalized Bayesian inference, robust NPE/SNL, or labeled calibration approaches. This makes claims of a major breakthrough unsupported.

Novelty is incremental: self-consistency losses were already proposed in prior work. The main new ingredient is applying them to unlabeled out-of-simulation data, which is a natural but not deeply developed extension.

Theoretical guarantees only cover cases where the likelihood or posterior is known. In the general ABI setting where both are unknown, the self-consistency loss alone is not strictly proper. The paper acknowledges this, but its main practical case remains without strong theoretical support.

Claims are substantially overstated. The abstract and discussion describe the work as a major breakthrough and near-perfect inference, but the evidence is a proof-of-concept on a simple synthetic Gaussian model.

Hyperparameters and training dynamics are insufficiently studied. The weighting parameter lambda, the proposal distribution p_C, and the number of self-consistency samples L are not ablated or analyzed in detail, despite being acknowledged as potentially important.
Reproducibility is limited: no code release is mentioned, no number of random seeds or repeated runs is clearly reported, and training time or computational cost is not discussed.

The method requires density evaluation and a known or surrogate likelihood, which restricts architectures and may not scale to free-form methods such as flow matching. This limitation is acknowledged but not addressed.

The paper is explicitly work in progress and promises future experiments. A top-tier venue requires a complete evaluation, not a preliminary proof-of-concept with several central claims deferred to a full version.

The estimated-likelihood experiments show noticeable posterior standard-deviation bias, sometimes with reversed sign, indicating the method is not yet robust in the very case where the theory is weakest. This is not sufficiently analyzed.

Positioning against related work is mostly qualitative. Closest methods are not empirically compared, and claimed advantages such as no accuracy-robustness trade-off are not convincingly demonstrated in finite-sample settings.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: robustness of amortized Bayesian inference under out-of-simulation data and model misspecification.
Proposes a clean semi-supervised formulation that combines standard simulation-based losses with Bayesian self-consistency losses on unlabeled data, preserving amortization and fast inference.

Provides theoretical results showing that self-consistency losses based on the Bayesian ratio are strictly proper when the likelihood is known, and that the semi-supervised loss is also strictly proper for arbitrary unlabeled data distribution p*(x).

The controlled normal-means experiments give strong empirical evidence that adding the self-consistency loss dramatically improves robustness, even with very few unlabeled observations and up to 100 parameters.
The paper is generally well-written and clearly positions the method relative to related work.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is limited to a single toy model class: the multivariate Gaussian normal-means problem. The authors themselves state this is a proof-of-concept and promise future experiments, so the core claims of broad robustness and a 'major breakthrough' are not yet supported.

No comparisons are made to existing robust ABI methods, such as post hoc corrections, calibration-set approaches, adversarial regularization, or generalized Bayesian inference. Without such baselines, claims that the approach avoids trade-offs or outperforms existing methods are not substantiated.

Despite motivation from real-world data, the unlabeled data are simulated from a shifted Gaussian distribution with a known likelihood. There is no evaluation on real data, common SBI benchmark tasks, or challenging posterior geometries, so applicability to realistic misspecification remains unclear.

The theoretical guarantees rely on a known likelihood. When the likelihood is unknown or estimated jointly, the self-consistency loss is not strictly proper without additional losses, and the experiments show noticeably worse performance. This limits the practical scope of the method, since real-world use often involves unknown likelihoods.

The strict-properness proofs are relatively straightforward extensions of the self-consistency definitions and do not resolve key practical issues such as joint posterior-likelihood learning, hyperparameter selection for the loss weight lambda, or computational cost.

The paper overstates its conclusions with phrases such as 'major breakthrough' and 'no existing ABI approach achieves similar degrees of robustness,' which are not justified by a single synthetic case study.
Evaluation lacks standard SBI benchmarks, real-data experiments, and sufficient comparison across scales and model classes; consequently, reproducibility and generalizability are limited.

strengths: Introduces a semi-supervised ABI framework that uses Bayesian self-consistency losses on unlabeled data, enabling robustness gains without requiring true parameters for real observations.

Provides theoretical results (Propositions 1-3) showing that the proposed self-consistency variance loss is strictly proper when the likelihood is known and the proposal distribution's support covers the posterior support.

Demonstrates substantial empirical improvements over standard NPE in a synthetic normal means problem and in a real air-passenger autoregressive case study, with posterior estimates close to Stan when using as few as four unlabeled datasets.
Maintains amortization and fast inference at test time; does not require post hoc corrections or adversarial defenses.
weaknesses: The core self-consistency loss was previously introduced for ABI; the novel contribution is mostly its application to unlabeled/out-of-simulation data, and the theoretical extensions are relatively straightforward. The claimed 'major breakthrough' is overstated.

Evaluation lacks comparisons to existing robust ABI methods (e.g., Ward et al. 2022, Wehenkel et al. 2024, Gloeckler et al. 2023, Huang et al. 2023, Gao et al. 2023). Only standard NPE and Stan are used, so the claim that no existing approach achieves similar robustness is unsupported.

The method's properness theory relies on a known likelihood; when both likelihood and posterior are learned, strict properness no longer holds and empirical gains are weaker. Many ABI applications have intractable likelihoods, limiting practical impact.

The air-traffic evaluation may be transductive/leaky: self-consistency is trained on unlabeled observations from countries that are later included in evaluation; especially for M=15, the test observations are seen during training, inflating robustness claims.
Important hyperparameters, especially the trade-off weight λ in the semi-supervised loss, are not reported or ablated, preventing assessment of robustness and reproducibility.

Reports and claims are not sufficiently supported by the limited experiments; no code is provided and no sensitivity analysis for λ, proposal distribution p_C, or number of unlabeled points beyond limited settings.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: robustness of amortized Bayesian inference under model misspecification and out-of-simulation observations.
Provides a clear semi-supervised formulation that combines standard simulation-based ABI losses with a Bayesian self-consistency loss on unlabeled data.
Offers theoretical propositions showing strict properness of self-consistency losses when the likelihood is known, with simple proofs.
Empirical results on the multivariate normal problem are promising: adding the self-consistency loss substantially improves posterior recovery far outside the training distribution.
The real-data air passenger case study is a useful step toward applying the idea beyond purely synthetic examples.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the self-consistency loss itself was introduced in prior work, and the extension to semi-supervised ABI with unlabeled data is relatively straightforward. The theoretical results are mostly immediate consequences of existing strict properness arguments.

The evaluation has a serious data leakage / unfair comparison issue in the real-data experiment: for M=15, the self-consistency loss is trained on real observations from all 15 countries, yet the metrics are then averaged over those same 15 countries. Even for M=8, several evaluated countries are included in the unlabeled training set, and seen/unseen countries are not separated. This undermines the central robustness claim on real data.

No comparisons to existing robust ABI methods despite an extensive related-work section. Baselines such as Ward et al., Siahkoohi et al., Gloeckler et al., Wehenkel et al., Gao et al., Huang et al., and Kelly et al. are not evaluated, so the claimed superiority or major advantage over prior work is unsupported.

The theory requires a known likelihood for strict properness. When the likelihood is estimated, as in an important practical setting, the guarantee vanishes and the method becomes heuristic. Many ABI problems have intractable likelihoods, so the scope is narrower than claimed.

The condition in Proposition 2 that p_C must cover the posterior support may not hold when p_C is chosen as the current approximate posterior during training. This and other finite-sample issues are not analyzed, leaving a gap between theory and practice.

The empirical study is narrow: only a normal means problem and a small autoregressive air-traffic dataset. There are no standard SBI benchmark tasks with challenging simulators, no high-dimensional real applications, and no evaluation of computational cost or scalability.
Key training details are missing: the value or tuning of the weighting parameter λ is not specified, there is no sensitivity analysis for λ, and no code or reproducibility statement is provided.

The paper repeatedly claims a 'major breakthrough' and 'remarkable improvements', but the evidence is insufficient for such strong claims, especially given the evaluation limitations and lack of baselines.

The method's reliance on evaluating p(x*|θ) for unlabeled data is not sufficiently discussed as a practical bottleneck. For complex mechanistic models, this likelihood may be unavailable or expensive, limiting applicability.
Some presentation issues remain (e.g., typos such as 'in pratice', inconsistent notation, and unclear separation of seen vs. unseen real data), which reduce clarity and reproducibility.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: robustness of amortized Bayesian inference under out-of-simulation data and model misspecification.
Proposes a simple semi-supervised extension that leverages self-consistency losses on unlabeled data, requiring no ground-truth parameters for real observations.

Provides theoretical results (Propositions 1–3) showing strict properness of the self-consistency loss and no trade-off between the standard simulation-based loss and the self-consistency loss for any unlabeled distribution.
Demonstrates striking improvements on the multivariate normal means problem, where standard NPE collapses but NPE+SC remains accurate far outside the training distribution.
Includes a real-world air passenger traffic case study showing that NPE+SC closely matches Stan, while standard NPE is often biased.
Maintains amortization and inference speed, avoiding post hoc corrections or loss of amortization.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the self-consistency loss was previously introduced, and the main extension here is applying it to unlabeled data, which is conceptually straightforward.
Evaluation is limited to two case studies, one synthetic and one relatively small real-world example; there are no standard SBI benchmark tasks or systematic misspecification experiments.

No comparison to existing robust ABI methods (e.g., calibration-based methods, post hoc corrections, adversarial regularization, or generalized Bayesian inference), making it difficult to assess relative merit.
The method generally requires a known likelihood or a learned likelihood approximation; the learned-likelihood experiments show degraded robustness and biased posterior standard deviations.

The air traffic experiment may have data leakage: when using M=15 countries, the self-consistency loss is trained on all countries and then evaluated on the same countries, so the near-perfect metrics do not demonstrate out-of-sample generalization.
The theoretical propositions rely on relatively strong assumptions (e.g., known likelihood, support conditions on p_C) and the proofs are straightforward.
The choice of proposal distribution p_C for the variance-based self-consistency loss is not ablated and is noted to materially affect training dynamics.
The paper overclaims a 'major breakthrough' and 'no existing ABI approach achieves similar robustness' despite limited evidence and missing baselines.
Reproducibility is only partially supported: no code release is mentioned, and computational costs are not discussed.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: robustness of amortized Bayesian inference under simulation gaps and out-of-distribution observations.
Proposes a semi-supervised ABI formulation that can leverage unlabeled data, including real observations, without requiring ground-truth parameters.
Provides theoretical propositions showing strict properness of the combined semi-supervised loss when the likelihood is known, establishing a no-trade-off result in that setting.
Empirical evaluation spans multiple domains: a controllable normal model, real air passenger time-series, high-dimensional Hodgkin-Huxley neuron data, and MNIST image denoising.
Demonstrates strong robustness gains over standard NPE, including accurate posterior approximations far outside the labeled and unlabeled training regions in several experiments.
Maintains amortized inference at test time, avoiding post-hoc MCMC corrections, which is practically appealing.
Includes useful ablations on parameter dimensionality, number of unlabeled observations, summary networks, and known vs. estimated likelihood in the toy setting.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited: the work extends existing self-consistency losses to a semi-supervised setting, and the key theoretical result (sum of strictly proper losses is strictly proper) is relatively straightforward.

The method fundamentally requires evaluating the likelihood p(x*|θ) for unlabeled observations. For many simulation-based inference problems the likelihood is intractable; if a neural likelihood surrogate is used, strict properness and the claimed no-trade-off guarantee no longer hold. This limitation is not emphasized enough in the abstract and main claims.

Missing empirical comparisons to existing robustness-focused ABI methods, such as Gloeckler et al. (2023), Ward et al. (2022), Wehenkel et al. (2024), Huang et al. (2023), or generalized Bayesian approaches. Only standard NPE is used as the ABI baseline, so claims about superiority over prior robustness methods are unsupported.

The MNIST denoising evaluation is largely qualitative (visual posterior means and standard deviations) and lacks quantitative metrics such as PSNR/SSIM, calibration measures, or comparisons to any denoising baseline.

Potential transductive/data-leakage concern in the air traffic experiment: Table 3 uses self-consistency data from all M=15 countries and evaluates on the same 15 countries, which likely overstates robustness. Even M=8 includes some evaluated countries?
No sensitivity analysis for the self-consistency weight λ, the number of consistency samples, or computational overhead is provided, despite claims about maintaining ABI speed.
The notation in Eq. (2) is unclear: C(·) is written without explicitly showing the expectation over θ used to compute the variance, making the loss difficult to parse from the main text.
Reproducibility is limited: no code repository or detailed experimental script is provided; hyperparameter choices for λ and training schedules are only partially specified.
Some writing/formatting issues remain, including repeated placeholder sentences such as 'The results of the proposed approach are shown in Fig. 2. ...' in the manuscript.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: robustness of amortized Bayesian inference under simulation gaps and model misspecification.
The proposed semi-supervised use of self-consistency losses on unlabeled data is conceptually simple and, if validated, could be practically useful.
The paper includes a theoretical discussion of strict properness for self-consistency losses, and the semi-supervised objective appears principled when the likelihood is known.
The empirical section covers multiple case studies, including a toy normal model, a real-world air traffic model, a Hodgkin-Huxley model, and MNIST image denoising, which demonstrates breadth.
The appendices provide substantial implementation details, including network architectures, training hyperparameters, and computational resources, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is incremental: the self-consistency loss itself was already introduced in prior work, and the paper mainly applies it to unlabeled data for robustness. The theoretical results are largely straightforward consequences of existing strict properness arguments.
The main text omits statements of Propositions 1 and 2, while later propositions depend on them. This makes the theoretical presentation incomplete and hard to assess.

The evaluation compares only standard NPE against NPE + self-consistency loss. It does not compare against existing robust ABI methods such as post-hoc corrections, calibration-based approaches, adversarial regularization, or generalized Bayesian inference, so claims of state-of-the-art robustness are unsupported.

The air traffic case study has a serious evaluation-protocol concern: the self-consistency loss is trained on real data from M countries, but metrics are then averaged over all 15 countries, including those used for self-consistency training. For M = 15, every test country was used during training, so the near-zero errors are not credible evidence of out-of-sample robustness.

The central claim that self-consistency losses introduce 'no trade-off' only holds when the likelihood is known exactly. When the likelihood is estimated, strict properness no longer holds, and the paper itself shows degraded calibration with reversed posterior standard-deviation bias in some settings. This substantially limits applicability to black-box simulators.

The method requires access to a likelihood or surrogate likelihood during training and fast density evaluations, which restricts the class of ABI methods it can be applied to and may add training overhead. The paper does not quantify training-time costs despite emphasizing ABI speed.

The empirical claims are stronger than the evidence: 'safe and reliable ABI', 'no trade-off', and 'notable robustness gains even for as few as four real-world observations' are not sufficiently supported by the experiments presented.

Several experimental results are difficult to interpret because the default configuration is not clearly identified, and the effect of the unlabeled data distribution is confounded with the evaluation distribution in places.

The manuscript contains apparent placeholder or repeated sentences ('The results of the proposed approach are shown in Fig. 2 ... Fig. 10') and missing proposition statements, which, if present in the submission, severely harm clarity and readiness for publication.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: robustness of amortized Bayesian inference under simulation gaps and model misspecification.
Proposes a semi-supervised approach that leverages unlabeled real/synthetic data via Bayesian self-consistency losses, avoiding the need for ground-truth parameters for those observations.
Provides theoretical results on strict properness for the proposed semi-supervised loss, extending existing self-consistency arguments.
Demonstrates strong empirical improvements over standard NPE across several case studies, including multivariate normal, air traffic, Hodgkin-Huxley, and MNIST denoising.
Method preserves amortization and inference speed, and can in principle be added to any standard simulation-based objective.
Shows robustness gains even with very few unlabeled observations (e.g., four) in some experiments, which is practically appealing.
weaknesses: Propositions 1 and 2 are referenced but never stated in the main text, making the theoretical development incomplete and hard to follow.
The manuscript contains repeated placeholder sentences ('The results of the proposed approach are shown in Fig. 2...' etc.) that indicate insufficient proofreading and care in preparation.

The air traffic case study appears to use the same countries for self-consistency training and evaluation (e.g., M=8 countries used in training, then metrics averaged over all 15 countries), which invalidates claims of out-of-sample robustness for that real-data example.

No empirical comparisons are provided against existing robust ABI methods (e.g., adversarial training, data-driven calibration, post hoc corrections, or generalized Bayesian inference), making it unclear whether the proposed approach is competitive.
The MNIST denoising experiment is evaluated only qualitatively; no quantitative image-quality metrics (e.g., PSNR, SSIM) are reported despite the high-dimensional setting.
The theoretical novelty is limited: strict properness of the sum of proper losses is a straightforward extension, and the core self-consistency loss is inherited from prior work.
The method requires a known or estimated likelihood; when both posterior and likelihood are unknown, strict properness does not hold, restricting the theoretical guarantee in practical ABI settings.

The 'no trade-off' claim is only partially supported empirically; there is no systematic evaluation showing that adding the self-consistency loss preserves in-distribution posterior accuracy across tasks.
Reproducibility is limited: no code or data release is mentioned, and some experimental details (e.g., default hyperparameters, held-out country splits) are ambiguous.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: robustness of amortized Bayesian inference on out-of-simulation/out-of-distribution data, using unlabeled observations without ground-truth parameters.

Provides theoretical results showing that Bayesian self-consistency losses are strictly proper and that the proposed semi-supervised loss remains strictly proper for any unlabeled data distribution, implying no trade-off with the simulation-based loss.

Empirical results across diverse tasks (multivariate normal, air traffic time series, Hodgkin-Huxley, MNIST denoising) show substantial improvements over standard NPE, often with very few unlabeled observations (e.g., M=4).
Maintains amortization and inference speed, avoids post hoc corrections, and does not require labeled calibration data.
Includes comparisons to Stan and several baselines (VAE, online NPE, Schmitt et al. 2024, NPE-MMD, NPE-DANN, NNPE) in the appendix, with detailed training and architecture information.
Demonstrates improved posterior predictive performance and more coherent uncertainty maps in high-dimensional time-series and image domains.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: self-consistency losses were introduced by Schmitt et al. (2024); the extension to unlabeled data is natural, and the theoretical propositions largely follow from standard proper scoring rules and Bayes' rule.

The method requires evaluating the likelihood p(x|θ) or a learned likelihood approximator. When the likelihood is estimated, strict properness no longer holds and empirical robustness degrades, limiting applicability to truly likelihood-free ABI settings.

Robustness baselines are not comprehensively integrated into the main paper: comparisons to NPE-MMD, NPE-DANN, NNPE, and labeled-calibration methods are relegated to the appendix and mostly evaluated on a simple 2D normal model rather than across all case studies.

Some evaluations rely on simulated unlabeled data (e.g., Hodgkin-Huxley) rather than real unlabeled observations; the MNIST misspecification is artificially induced; and the air-traffic comparison uses Stan under the same assumed model rather than real-world ground truth.

The self-consistency weight λ requires scheduling and can cause training instability, especially in high-dimensional settings, but sensitivity and training-cost implications are not systematically analyzed.
Reproducibility is weakened by the missing/blank code URL ('code is available at') in the abstract despite the reproducibility statement.
Claims about robustness far outside the training distribution are strongest only in the controlled normal-means toy problem, with less direct evidence in complex real-data regimes.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: improving the robustness of amortized Bayesian inference under simulation gaps, model misspecification, and out-of-distribution observations.
The proposed extension of self-consistency losses to unlabeled data is intuitive and straightforward to implement on top of existing neural posterior estimation pipelines with normalizing flows.
The theoretical analysis is clearly presented and provides formal strict-properness results under known likelihood, which helps clarify when the self-consistency loss targets the analytic posterior.

The empirical section covers a reasonable range of applications, including a toy normal model, real air-traffic time series, a Hodgkin-Huxley model, and MNIST denoising, with some evidence that robustness improves even with few unlabeled observations.
The appendix provides detailed architectures, hyperparameters, and experimental setups, which supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. Self-consistency losses were previously introduced by Schmitt et al. (2024), and the main contribution here is adapting them to unlabeled data. Propositions 1-3 are largely straightforward consequences of strict properness and do not constitute deep technical advances.

The central theoretical guarantees only hold when the likelihood is known. In most ABI applications, the likelihood is intractable, so the method must estimate it jointly with the posterior. The paper acknowledges that strict properness fails when both posterior and likelihood are unknown, and that degenerate solutions can minimize the SC loss. This directly undermines the claims of 'strictly proper', 'no trade-off', and targeting the analytic posterior in the practical settings where the method is most needed.

The variance-based self-consistency loss assumes that the proposal distribution p_C(theta) covers the support of the true posterior for strict properness. In practice p_C is the current approximate posterior, which may be far from the true posterior, especially early in training or under strong distribution shift. The paper does not adequately address this assumption or provide diagnostics for when it is violated.

The claim that there is no trade-off between the simulation-based loss and the self-consistency loss is misleading in finite-data, finite-capacity, and misspecified regimes. The need for lambda scheduling, joint training, and the observed instability when using SC alone indicate practical trade-offs and optimization challenges that are not captured by the idealized theory.

The evaluation of robustness under real misspecification is weak. For the air-traffic and normal-means case studies, the reference method (Stan) assumes the same statistical model, so the comparison primarily verifies computational approximation to a possibly misspecified posterior rather than correctness under model misspecification. Stronger evidence would require settings where the true data-generating process is known to differ from the assumed model.

Baselines are insufficient for a paper claiming robustness in ABI. The main comparisons are against standard NPE and Stan. Other robust ABI methods are tested only in a low-dimensional toy setting in the appendix, and some are dismissed as targeting different posteriors. Important baselines such as Wehenkel et al. (2024) calibration, robust SBI methods, or simple unlabeled-data fine-tuning/augmentation are missing across the main case studies.

The MNIST and Hodgkin-Huxley experiments are largely qualitative or indirect. MNIST denoising lacks standard quantitative metrics such as MSE, PSNR, SSIM, or calibration measures, and compares only NPLE vs NPLE+SC. Hodgkin-Huxley reports posterior predictive bias but not parameter recovery or calibration against ground truth or MCMC.

The claim that unlabeled data can originate from 'any source' is overstated. The SC loss requires evaluating p(x*|theta) under the model (or a surrogate likelihood), so the unlabeled data must be compatible with the assumed likelihood. For complex simulators, surrogate likelihood errors may propagate into the SC loss and degrade robustness.

Several experiments use simulated unlabeled data rather than genuinely real unlabeled data, which weakens the real-world applicability claims. For example, the normal-means and Hodgkin-Huxley unlabeled sets are generated from known distributions rather than real observations.

The experimental comparisons may be biased by small simulation budgets for the NPE baseline. For instance, air-traffic NPE uses only 1024 simulations, while the appendix occasionally uses larger budgets for other methods. More carefully equalized training budgets and tuning would be needed to isolate the benefit of SC losses.

The manuscript overstates the safety and robustness implications. Since the method does not provide guarantees when the likelihood is estimated and the model is misspecified, claims about enabling widespread and safe application of ABI are not adequately supported.
Minor issues: the code URL appears incomplete in the manuscript, and some references contain typographical errors. These are not central but affect reproducibility and polish.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: robustness of amortized Bayesian inference under simulation gaps, model misspecification, and domain shift.
It proposes a clean semi-supervised extension of self-consistency losses to unlabeled data, allowing training on real observations without ground-truth parameters.
The theoretical analysis establishes strict properness of self-consistency losses (Propositions 1-4) and argues no trade-off with simulation-based losses, which is useful and reassuring.

The empirical evaluation spans diverse case studies: conjugate normal means with analytic posterior, real air traffic autoregressive model, Hodgkin-Huxley neuron time series, and high-dimensional MNIST denoising.
Results show substantial robustness gains, sometimes with very few unlabeled observations (M=4), while maintaining amortized inference speed.
The paper includes comparisons to relevant baselines (NPE, Stan, NPE-DANN, NPE-MMD, NNPE, VAE, Schmitt et al.) and provides reproducibility details/code.
weaknesses: The core novelty is somewhat incremental: self-consistency losses and their properness were previously introduced by Schmitt et al. (2024) and Ivanova et al. (2024); the main new component is using them on unlabeled real data, which is a natural extension.

Strict properness relies on knowing or reliably estimating the likelihood; when both posterior and likelihood are unknown, the SC loss is not strictly proper and the theory no longer directly supports the method. The estimated-likelihood experiments show remaining bias, especially in posterior standard deviation.

Practical applicability to fully implicit likelihood models is limited: the method needs density evaluations of the likelihood (or a surrogate/neural likelihood) during training, which can be expensive or inaccurate.

Some evaluation is not fully quantitative: the MNIST denoising case study mainly reports visual results and uncertainty maps without standard quantitative image metrics, and comparisons to robustness-specific UDA methods are restricted to the normal-means toy problem.
Hyperparameter choice (lambda scheduling) is somewhat ad hoc and important for stabilization, which may limit ease of use in high-dimensional settings.
Claims of 'no trade-off' are theoretically justified asymptotically but may be too strong under finite model capacity, finite training data, and nonconvex optimization.
Minor reproducibility issue: the abstract's code link appears incomplete/placeholder in the provided manuscript.
